transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

Probably not. A buzz or hum from an induction hob on maximum power is commonly normal, particularly with a large, heavy or multi-layer stockpot. The pan base can vibrate slightly in the magnetic field, and the hob cooling fan may add to the sound. 1. Turn the same zone down from high to a mid setting. If the noise falls with the power level and cooking remains normal, that strongly supports normal induction noise.
2. Try another flat-based magnetic pan on that zone. If the sound is only with the stockpot, its base is resonating or may be slightly warped; that is not usually a hob fault.
3. Make sure the base and glass are clean and dry, and the pan sits flat. A magnet should stick firmly to the base. Stop using the hob and arrange service if there is loud cracking, a burning/hot-plastic smell, sparking, a fault code, or it switches itself off. Otherwise, noise limited to a big pot on high is generally normal rather than a sign it is about to fail.

Thanks, that's reassuring. I tried a few of those: it's much quieter at 6 and below, and my heavy cast iron pot is quiet on the same zone. The buzzing only happens with the new stockpot (and a cheap frying pan). No error codes or cutting out, and no burning smell. Is the pot just the problem then?

Yes — the evidence points very strongly to the pans, not the hob. Because the cast-iron pot is quiet on the same zone, while both the new stockpot and cheap frying pan buzz, the hob is producing normal induction power and those pan bases are resonating at higher settings. A little buzzing at high power is harmless. The stockpot may be made from thinner or layered steel, or its base may not be perfectly flat; the cheap frying pan is likely doing the same. It does not mean the hob is about to fail. 1. With the pans cold and the hob off, place each on a flat worktop or the unpowered glass and gently press opposite edges. If it rocks or spins slightly, the base is not flat enough and will be more prone to buzzing.
2. Check the base is clean and dry. A firmly magnetic, flat, heavier-based pan usually runs more quietly. If the pan sits flat and cooks evenly, you can keep using it — reducing from maximum to around 6–8 is the practical cure for the noise. Replace or return the stockpot only if the noise is unacceptable, it becomes distorted, or it heats unevenly. Service for the hob is not indicated unless the noise starts with known-good pans too, or you get a fault code, cut-out, burning smell, cracking or sparking.
I pressed the pot on the worktop and I'm not sure it rocks, but the base is a sandwich base, maybe slightly smaller than the ring. Could that be why it buzzes?

Yes. A sandwich base can be exactly why it buzzes: its bonded layers can vibrate very slightly in the induction field, particularly at maximum power. A base that is a little smaller than the zone can also make that resonance more noticeable, although it is not harmful if the pan is still recognised and heats evenly. The strongest clue is that the cast-iron pot is quiet on the same zone, while the stockpot and cheaper frying pan buzz, and the sound drops at setting 6 or below. That makes a hob fault very unlikely. You do not need to prove whether it rocks. With the pan cold, the useful practical check is whether it heats evenly: put a shallow layer of water in it and heat on a moderate setting. If it warms normally without obvious cool areas or repeated pan-detection problems, the pan is suitable to use. Keep it below full power if the noise is annoying. A markedly undersized magnetic base may heat less evenly and be noisier, but a slightly smaller base is usually fine. Consider returning the stockpot only if it becomes distorted, heats poorly, loses pan detection, or the noise is unacceptable. There is no present sign that the hob is about to fail.

candidates: Normal induction cookware resonance at high power (high)
Stockpot base is uneven or not fully compatible with induction (medium)
Induction fan or power electronics fault (low)
